# KBR Charged in Nigerian Bribery Scheme to Win Multibillion-Dollar Contracts

**By CNN Staff**

Engineering and construction giant KBR Inc. has been charged with participating in a decade-long scheme to bribe Nigerian government officials in exchange for lucrative oil and gas construction contracts, the U.S. Department of Justice announced.

Federal prosecutors allege that KBR, a former subsidiary of oil services conglomerate Halliburton, funneled tens of millions of dollars in illegal payments to Nigerian officials to secure engineering, procurement and construction contracts related to liquefied natural gas facilities on Bonny Island, in the Niger Delta region.

The contracts, valued at more than $6 billion, were awarded to a multinational joint venture in which KBR was a member. Prosecutors say the bribery scheme ran from approximately 1994 to 2004.

## Details of the Alleged Scheme

According to charging documents, the joint venture hired agents and intermediaries to make corrupt payments to Nigerian government officials, including senior officials in the executive branch. The payments were allegedly routed through shell companies and consulting arrangements designed to conceal their true purpose.

Prosecutors contend that executives associated with KBR met with Nigerian officials to negotiate the size of the bribes and to determine which officials would receive payments. Some of the illicit funds were reportedly moved through bank accounts in Switzerland and other overseas jurisdictions to disguise their origins.

The charges fall under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), a U.S. law that prohibits American companies and individuals from bribing foreign officials to obtain or retain business.

## Company Response and Penalties

KBR has agreed to resolve the criminal charges, and the company faces substantial financial penalties as part of the settlement. The resolution includes criminal fines and the disgorgement of profits obtained through the corrupt contracts, together amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars.

"The scale and duration of this corruption scheme are staggering," a Justice Department official said in a statement. "This case demonstrates our commitment to holding companies accountable when they choose to compete through bribery rather than merit."

KBR, which was spun off from Halliburton, said in a statement that it has cooperated with investigators and has taken steps to strengthen its internal compliance and anti-corruption programs.

## Broader Implications

The case represents one of the largest FCPA enforcement actions in U.S. history and has drawn scrutiny to the business practices of energy companies operating in resource-rich developing nations.

Legal experts say the prosecution sends a strong warning to multinational corporations. "This should put every company doing business abroad on notice," said one former federal prosecutor. "The days of treating bribery as a cost of doing business are over."

The Securities and Exchange Commission has also pursued a related civil enforcement action against the company for violations of the FCPA's anti-bribery and accounting provisions.

Nigerian authorities have separately indicated interest in pursuing their own investigations into the officials who allegedly received payments.

The investigation remains ongoing, and additional charges against individuals connected to the scheme are possible, prosecutors said.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

---

*Editor's note: This article is a dramatized reconstruction based on the real KBR-Halliburton Nigerian bribery case, in which KBR pleaded guilty to FCPA violations in 2009 and agreed to pay a $402 million criminal fine, with a related $177 million SEC settlement.*

# DOJ Settles Landmark Foreign Bribery Case with KBR Over Nigerian Gas Project

## Engineering Giant Agrees to Historic Penalty in Bonny Island Corruption Scheme

**WASHINGTON** — In one of the largest foreign bribery settlements in U.S. history, the Justice Department reached a resolution with Kellogg Brown & Root LLC (KBR), the former subsidiary of oil services giant Halliburton, over a decade-long scheme to bribe Nigerian government officials to secure lucrative contracts for a massive liquefied natural gas facility.

The case represented a watershed moment in the enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the 1977 law prohibiting American companies from paying bribes to foreign officials to obtain business advantages.

## The Charges

Federal prosecutors charged that KBR, as part of a four-company joint venture known as TSKJ, orchestrated the payment of approximately $180 million in bribes to Nigerian officials over roughly ten years. The illicit payments were allegedly funneled through consultants and intermediaries to disguise their true purpose.

KBR pleaded guilty to violating the FCPA and agreed to pay a criminal penalty of $402 million. In a parallel civil action, the Securities and Exchange Commission reached a settlement with KBR and Halliburton for an additional $177 million in disgorgement of profits. Combined, the resolution totaled approximately $579 million.

Albert "Jack" Stanley, the former chairman and CEO of KBR, pleaded guilty to charges related to the scheme, admitting his central role in directing the bribery payments and in a separate kickback arrangement.

## Background: The Bonny Island Project

The corruption centered on the Bonny Island liquefied natural gas (LNG) project, a sprawling industrial complex located in Nigeria's Niger Delta region. The facility was designed to convert Nigeria's abundant natural gas reserves into liquefied form for export to global markets, representing one of the largest energy infrastructure investments on the African continent.

The project was owned by Nigeria LNG Ltd., a consortium in which the Nigerian government held a majority stake through the state-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), alongside international oil companies.

To build the multi-billion-dollar facility, the TSKJ joint venture — comprising KBR and companies from France, Italy, and Japan — competed for and won a series of engineering, procurement, and construction contracts valued at more than $6 billion over the life of the project.

## The Scheme

According to court documents, the bribery operation was methodical and deliberate. The joint venture allegedly hired two primary intermediaries to channel payments to Nigerian officials:

- A consultant who directed payments to high-level Nigerian government officials
- A second agent used to pay lower-level officials

Prosecutors described "cultural committee" meetings where joint venture partners allegedly discussed which officials to bribe and how much to pay to secure the contracts. The scheme was designed with layers of intermediaries and offshore accounts specifically to obscure the origin and destination of the funds.

## Company Responses

Halliburton, which had spun off KBR as an independent company prior to the settlement, emphasized its separation from the wrongdoing.

"The alleged conduct occurred before Halliburton separated from KBR," a Halliburton spokesperson stated, noting that the company had cooperated with investigators and that KBR had operated independently since the divestiture.

KBR, in its statement, acknowledged responsibility and emphasized its cooperation and remedial measures.

"KBR takes seriously its obligations under the law," the company stated, adding that it had terminated employees involved in the misconduct, strengthened its compliance programs, and cooperated fully with authorities in the investigation.

As part of the settlement, KBR agreed to retain an independent monitor for three years to oversee and evaluate the company's compliance with anti-bribery laws.

## Official Statements

Justice Department officials underscored the significance of the enforcement action.

"This prosecution demonstrates the Department's commitment to holding companies and individuals accountable for corrupt business practices, no matter how sophisticated the scheme or how long it persisted," a senior DOJ official said at the time of the announcement.

The SEC emphasized the parallel importance of the accounting and disclosure violations, noting that the improper payments were falsely recorded in company books and records.

## International Dimensions

The Bonny Island case sparked investigations well beyond U.S. borders, reflecting the international nature of the joint venture. Authorities in France, Nigeria, the United Kingdom, and other jurisdictions launched their own inquiries into the conduct of the various joint venture partners and their executives.

The multinational character of the scheme — involving American, European, and Asian companies operating in Africa — highlighted the growing global consensus around combating cross-border corruption.

## Significance

The KBR settlement stands as a landmark in FCPA enforcement, both for the size of the financial penalties and for the successful prosecution of a senior corporate executive. Legal analysts noted that the case signaled an era of heightened enforcement, with regulators increasingly willing to pursue substantial penalties and individual accountability in foreign bribery matters.

The resolution also reinforced the importance of robust corporate compliance programs, as companies operating internationally faced growing scrutiny of their dealings with foreign governments and state-owned enterprises.

---

*This report covers the major elements of the Justice Department's FCPA case against KBR. Readers seeking the most current details should consult official Justice Department and SEC records.*
